title: A Combined Regenerative Approach for Managing Gingival Recession
html:
Written by:
Annemarie Olga Athansios, DMD, MDS
George Athansios, DMD, MDS
Howard Drew, DMD
Gus Cappetta, DMD
Paul S. Rosen, DMD, MS

Abstract

This case series aims to evaluate the effectiveness of the protocol described by McGuire and Scheyer1for treating gingival recession defects. This involved the application of recombinant human platelet-derived growth factor-BB (rhPDGF-BB) combined with β-tricalcium phosphate (β-TCP) beneath a porous wound dressing and a coronally advanced flap (CAF). Four patients are reported on who presented to the Rutgers University School of Dental Medicine with single and multiple RT-I (Miller Class I and Class II) recession defects in both the maxilla and mandible. Healing outcomes were assessed based on the degree of root coverage (complete, partial, or none), gain in gingival thickness (GT), and increase in keratinized tissue width (KTW). In one patient, a CT scan obtained ten months post-treatment allowed assessment of the regenerative outcome. This demonstrated hard tissue gain on the prior exposed labial root surface.

INTRODUCTION

Gingival recession (GR), defined as the apical displacement of the gingival margin resulting in exposure of the root surface, is a common clinical acquired deformity encountered in daily dental practice. It can affect patients of all ages but is particularly prevalent in older populations; epidemiological studies report that at least one site with 1 mm or more of gingival recession is found in approximately 40% of young adults and up to 88% of older adults.2 The causes of GR are multifactorial, including periodontal disease, traumatic toothbrushing, anatomical factors such as thin gingival phenotype, orthodontic movement, or restorative procedures that impinge on the biological width. While gingival recession may sometimes appear benign, its clinical implications are significant. Patients often present with esthetic concerns—especially in the anterior region—as well as tooth hypersensitivity, increased risk of root caries, and plaque accumulation on exposed root surfaces. More critically, untreated recession may progress, contributing to further patient dissatisfaction, attachment loss, root exposure, and eventual tooth mobility or loss if left unaddressed.

For decades, periodontists have relied on techniques such as the subepithelial connective tissue graft (SCTG)—widely regarded as the gold standard—for root coverage.

These techniques, often combined with coronally advanced flaps or tunneling methods, yield favorable outcomes but are not without limitations. Donor site morbidity, as well as extended surgical time, potential complications like injury to the greater palatine artery, and variable esthetic results highlight the need for alternatives.

Minimally invasive regenerative approaches are gaining traction, especially those that incorporate biologics to enhance healing. The American Academy of Periodontology (AAP) convened a Best Evidence Consensus (BEC) workshop in 2022 and concluded that biologics such as autologous blood-derived products, enamel matrix derivative (EMD), and recombinant human platelet-derived growth factor-BB (rhPDGF-BB) are viable adjuncts in mucogingival surgery.

Among these, rhPDGF-BB combined with beta-tricalcium phosphate (β-TCP) has demonstrated promising regenerative capabilities, including the formation of Sharpey’s fibers, cementum, and alveolar bone in sites with isolated gingival recession.3

This case series evaluates the clinical application of rhPDGF-BB and β-TCP in the treatment of RT1 (Miller Class I and II) gingival recession defects using a coronally advanced flap (CAF). Four patients with single or multiple defects in the maxilla and mandible were treated at Rutgers University School of Dental Medicine (RSDM) following the protocols established by McGuire and Scheyer and McGuire et al.1,3

Materials and Methods

Four patients presented to RSDM for evaluation of tooth sensitivity and gingival recession. After thorough clinical examinations, they were diagnosed with single and multiple RT-I (Miller Class I and Class II) recession defects in the maxilla and/or mandible. A minimally invasive regenerative approach, as described by McGuire and Scheyer,1 was selected to maximize patient comfort and reduce postoperative discomfort. All patients received detailed post-op instructions and were scheduled for followup appointments to monitor healing and assess treatment effectiveness.

Case 1

A 61-year-old female with a history of controlled hypertension presented to the RSDM clinic with a chief complaint of cold sensitivity in the upper right maxilla (Figure 1a). Clinical examination revealed that tooth No. 6 had an RT-I (Miller Class II) recession defect, accompanied by NCCL-A+.4The defect was treated using a combination of rhPDGF-BB and β-TCP, along with a collagen wound dressing and a coronally advanced flap (CAF).

Surgical procedure

After administration of local anesthesia, the exposed root surface was prepared using chisels, curettes, finishing burs, and an EDTA solution. An intracrevicular incision was made at the affected tooth, and 2 oblique releasing incisions were placed at least 1 mm from the gingival margin of adjacent teeth, extending into the alveolar mucosa (Figure 2a). A full-thickness flap was raised approximately 3 to 4 mm apical to the bone dehiscence, followed by a partial-thickness dissection to allow coronal advancement.

The interdental papillae were de-epithelialized. The rhPDGF-BB solution was applied to the exposed root surface and the coronal periodontal ligament fibers. A small quantity of β-TCP saturated with rhPDGF-BB was placed below the CEJ, covering the denuded root and extending 2 to 3 mm onto adjacent bone (Figure 2b). A bioabsorbable collagen wound dressing saturated with rhPDGF-BB was placed over the grafted area (Figure 2c). The CAF was then positioned at the CEJ and secured to the de-epithelialized papillae with 5-0 vicryl sutures using a single interrupted technique (Figure 2d).

Clinical Outcomes

The surgical site healed uneventfully. The patient reported minimal to no discomfort. Complete root coverage was observed at both 3- and 10-month followup appointments (Figure 1b).

A CBCT scan suggested approximately 0.9 mm of hard tissue gain on the buccal surface (Figure 3).

Case 2

A 62-year-old African-American female presented to RSDM with a chief complaint of cold sensitivity in her upper left quadrant. Clinical examination revealed several teeth with RT-I and RT-II recession defects (Figure 4). Due to a history of dental anxiety, the patient preferred a minimally invasive treatment. McGuire’s technique was selected for root coverage.3 In the site adjacent to an edentulous area with posterior bone loss, root coverage was not expected.

The surgical steps mirrored those described in Case 1. The CAF was advanced and secured using a composite button on the buccal surfaces of the teeth (Figure 4e). The patient reported minimal postoperative discomfort and no sensitivity at the 8-month followup (Figure 4f).

Case 3

A patient presented to RSDM with a chief complaint of cold sensitivity in the lower right quadrant. Tooth No. 28 was diagnosed with an RT-I (Miller Class I) recession defect (Figure 5a). McGuire and Scheyer’s CAF technique1 was employed (Figures 5b to 5e). Complete root coverage was achieved, and the patient reported no sensitivity at the 8-month, post-op followup.

Case 4

A healthy young male presented to RSDM with a similar complaint of cold sensitivity in the upper left quadrant. Tooth No. 28 was diagnosed with an RT-I (Miller Class I) recession defect (Figure 6a). The CAF technique employed in the previous case was utilized again (Figures 6b to 6e). The patient experienced complete root coverage and reported no sensitivity at the 8-month followup.

DISCUSSION

McGuire and Scheyer’s technique1 combines the coronally advanced flap (CAF) with regenerative biomaterials to promote tissue regeneration and enhance periodontal health. Recombinant human platelet-derived growth factor-BB (rhPDGF-BB) is a synthetic version of the body’s natural wound-healing protein, PDGF-BB. This biologic agent is known to be mitogenic and chemotactic for periodontal ligament cells and osteoblasts and also stimulates angiogenesis. An animal study has demonstrated rhPDGF-BB’s ability to promote regeneration.4 In 2009, McGuire3 published landmark human histologic evidence of true periodontal regeneration in recession defect treatment using rhPDGF-BB, highlighting the transformative potential of biologic-based periodontal therapy.

This case series illustrates that the use of rhPDGF-BB combined with β-TCP and collagen matrix in a minimally invasive surgical approach can lead to highly favorable clinical outcomes in the treatment of RT-I and select RT-II gingival recession defects. While no histologic analysis was performed in these cases, one patient exhibited a radiographic gain of approximately 0.9 mm of hard tissue at the 10-month followup.

These clinical results support the growing body of evidence that biological agents such as rhPDGF-BB can improve both soft and hard tissue outcomes when used in combination with surgical techniques like CAF. Compared to traditional autogenous grafting, this approach offers several benefits, including shorter surgical time, decreased patient morbidity, and improved post-op comfort—an important consideration in patient-centered care.

Furthermore, the minimally invasive nature of McGuire and Scheyer’s technique1 aligns with contemporary trends in periodontology that prioritize aesthetics, patient comfort, and biologically driven outcomes. For patients with dental anxiety, systemic health considerations, or aesthetic demands, biologically enhanced minimally invasive techniques offer a predictable and less traumatic alternative to traditional grafting procedures aimed at root coverage.

In summary, the present case series demonstrates that most RT-I and some RT-II recession defects can be effectively treated using a combination of CAF and rhPDGF-BB with β-TCP. As the field continues to evolve, the integration of biologic agents into soft tissue procedures will continue to shift the paradigm toward regenerative, patient-friendly treatment protocols with long-term clinical stability and aesthetic success.

ABOUT THE AUTHORS

Dr. Annemarie O. Athansios earned her DMD with honors from Rutgers School of Dental Medicine (RSDM), where she was awarded the “Professionalism Award” for her exceptional ethics and the “Give Kids a Smile Award” for her volunteer contributions. She then completed a 3-year residency in Periodontics, obtaining a Master of Dental Science degree from Rutgers. During her postgraduate training, Dr. Athansios served as chief resident, presented at the Tri-school Symposium, graduated from the Institute of Advanced Laser Dentistry, and received the Michael J. Deasy Endowed Scholarship. Currently, she practices in Nutley and Cedar Grove, NJ, and is an active member of the American Academy of Periodontology, American Dental Association, and New Jersey Dental Association. Dr. Athansios also serves as the President of the Essex County Dental Society. Passionate about education, she dedicates her time to mentoring high school and college students interested in dentistry and participates in mission trips to provide dental care to underserved communities in Bolivia, the Dominican Republic, and Egypt.

Dr. George Athansios earned his DMD at Rutgers School of Dental Medicine, formally UMDNJ, and soon after, practiced as a General Dentist for 14 years. After becoming a Fellow of the AGD, a Fellow of the AAID, and a Diplomate of the American Board of Oral Implantology, Dr. Athansios returned to Rutgers School of Dental Medicine to complete his periodontal residency. Today, Dr. Athansios is an active member of the American Academy of Periodontology, American Dental Association and New Jersey Dental Association. He is a past President of the Essex County Dental Society and currently sits as a Trustee on the Board of NJDA. Dr. Athansios has participated on missions to Egypt, Ethiopia and Bolivia. Dr. George has a private practice in Cedar Grove and West Milford, NJ. He can be reached at georgedmd@gmail.com.

Dr. Howard Drew is a professor, the director of implantology, and the vice chairman in the Department of Periodontics at RSDM. He received his doctorate and degree in Periodontics from RSDM. He has been awarded the RSDM Excellence in Teaching Award, Stuart D. Cook Master Educators Guild Award, and the prestigious American Academy of Periodontology Educator Award. Dr. Drew was inducted into the American College of Dentists, and he was awarded the RSDM Alumni Association Decade (1980s) Award. He has written for more than 35 publications and has lectured throughout the country. He was in full-time clinical practice for more than 25 years. He can be reached at drewhj@sdm.rutgers.edu.

Dr. Gus Cappetta is PG Director and an assistant professor in the department of periodontics at RSDM. He can be reached at cappeteg@sdm.rutgers.edu.

Dr. Paul Rosen maintains full-time private practices in both Yardley, Pa and New York, NY limited to periodontics, surgical implant placement and regenerative therapy. He also has appointments as a clinical professor of Periodontics at both Rutgers University School of Dental Medicine and the University of Maryland Dental School as well as being an adjunct professor at New York University College of Dentistry. Dr. Rosen is a Diplomate of the American Board of Periodontology and has served in the past as an Examiner for the Board as well. Dr. Rosen is a reviewer for and serves on the editorial advisory boards for a number of dental journals. He has authored/co-authored a number of articles and several book chapters on periodontal regeneration, implants and interrelated orthodontic-periodontal care and lectured both nationally and internationally on the subjects of dental implants and regeneration for both teeth and dental implants. Dr. Rosen is honored for his work by receiving a number of prestigious awards including the American Academy of Periodontology’s Master Clinician Award in 2015, the Northeastern Society of Periodontists Isidor Hirschfeld Award for Clinical Excellence in 2016, and the Distinguished Alumnus Award for Professional Achievement from the University of Maryland Dental School in 2020.
